lessons.title: io — "I," the pronoun Italian loves to leave out

segments.text: Before you introduce yourself, meet io — "I." It's a small word with a famous English cousin, and a surprising habit: Italian usually drops it.
io-glide — io = EE-oh, two quick vowels gliding together, stress the first: EE-oh.
io = "I," worn down from Latin ego — which English borrowed whole:
ego — literally Latin "I" (your sense of self).
egoist, egotist, egocentric — all built on that "I."
Its Romance siblings: Spanish yo, Portuguese eu, French je — every one a child of ego.

Here's the Italian habit worth learning now: the verb ending already tells you who's speaking, so the pronoun is usually left out. Sto bene ("I'm well") needs no io — the -o of sto is "I." You add io only for emphasis or contrast:
Io sto bene — e tu? — "I'm fine — and you?"
Spanish (yo) and Portuguese (eu) do exactly the same. English can't: it must say "I" every time. So learning Italian means learning to trust the verb ending and let the pronoun go.

segments.text: What Latin word is io from, and what English words share it? (Ego — ego, egoist.) Why does Italian usually drop io? (The verb ending already says who.) When do you keep it? (For emphasis/contrast.) Next: use it to introduce yourself — mi chiamo.
Like Spanish and French, Italian doesn't say "my name is." It says "I call myself" — mi chiamo. Same reflexive trick, same clāmāre root as Spanish me llamo.
ch-hard-k — Italian ch is a hard k (the opposite of English!): so chiamo = KYAH-moh, not "chee-." (Italian softens c to ch-sound only before e/i; the h in chi is there precisely to keep it hard.)
mi chiamo = mee KYAH-moh.
mi chiamo = mi ("myself") + chiamo ("I call") becomes "I call myself." Then the name: Mi chiamo Marco — "I call myself Marco."
The verb is chiamarsi ("to call oneself"), from Latin clāmāre, "to cry out, to call." That root shouts through English:
claim, exclaim, proclaim, acclaim, clamor — all "calling out."

Its Romance siblings all name people the same way: Spanish llamarse (me llamo), Portuguese chamar-se (me chamo) — the cl- softening to ll- (Spanish) or ch- (Italian/Portuguese). One Latin "call," three naming verbs.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the reflexive, and the dropping of io

segments.text: chiamo alone is "I call [someone else]"; mi chiamo is "I call myself" — reflexive, the action looping back on you. The pronoun changes with the person: mi chiamo (I) becomes ti chiami (you) becomes si chiama (he/she/formal). And notice: no io — the -o ending already says "I." (You met that pro-drop last lesson.)

segments.text: What does mi chiamo literally mean? ("I call myself.") What Latin verb is chiamarsi from, and its English cousins? (clāmāre — claim, exclaim, clamor.) How is Italian ch pronounced? (A hard k.) Next: ask it back — Come ti chiami?

lessons.title: Come ti chiami? — "what's your name?"
lessons.gloss: what's your name? (informal); formal Come si chiama?

segments.text: You have both pieces: come ("how," from your how-are-you chapter) and chiamarsi ("to call oneself"). Like Spanish and French, Italian asks the name with "how", not "what": how do you call yourself?
Come ti chiami? = "What's your name?" (informal) literally: "How do you call yourself?"
come = "how" ( from quōmodo; you met it in Come stai?).
ti = "yourself" (the reflexive, matching mi becomes ti).
chiami = "you call" (the tu form of chiamarsi).
Two registers — the same tu / Lei split you learned in Chapter 2:

utterances: register: informal (tu). question: Come ti chiami?
register: formal (Lei). question: Come si chiama?

segments.text: Only the reflexive pronoun and the ending move: ti chiami becomes si chiama — the identical pattern to mi chiamo becomes si chiama. The whole exchange:
— Come ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Marco. E tu?
Note Italian asks the name with come ("how"), exactly like Spanish ¿cómo se llama? and French comment vous appelez-vous? — the name is a matter of how you're called, not what you are.

segments.text: What does Come ti chiami? literally ask? ("How do you call yourself?") What changes for the formal Lei version? (ti chiami becomes si chiama.) Which "how" word is it built on? (come from quōmodo.) Next: the reply when you meet — piacere.

lessons.title: piacere — "pleased to meet you," i.e. "a pleasure"

segments.text: Names exchanged, you close the introduction with one warm word: piacere — literally "a pleasure." It's the twin of a word you'd say in Portuguese, and it's pure Latin please.
soft-c — piacere = pya-CHEH-reh: here c is before e, so it's soft (ch), and the ia glides: pya-CHE-re.
piacere = "a pleasure" (and, as a verb, "to please"), from Latin placēre, "to please, to be pleasing." Said on meeting someone, it's short for "[it's] a pleasure [to meet you]."
That placēre root is thoroughly at home in English:
please, pleasure, pleasant — the direct line.
complacent ("pleased with oneself"), complaisant, placid (pleased becomes calm).
And across the family, "pleased to meet you" is built from the same idea nearly everywhere:
Portuguese prazer ( from placēre too — its twin).
French enchanté (a different image — "enchanted").
Spanish mucho gusto ("much pleasure," but from gustus, "taste" — a different Latin root).
Piacere stands alone — you just say it, with a small nod, as you shake hands. For a touch more you can say molto piacere ("much pleasure") or piacere di conoscerti ("pleasure to know you").

lessons.title: Practice — introducing yourself in Italian
lessons.gloss: introducing yourself in Italian, formal and informal

segments.text: No new words. io, mi chiamo, come ti chiami, piacere now assemble into a real first meeting — run it formally and informally until the register swap is automatic. This slots between your greetings (Ch. 1–2) and farewells (Ch. 4).
Informal (a peer):
— Ciao! Come ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Marco. E tu? — Giulia. Piacere! — Piacere!
Formal (a stranger — Lei):
— Buongiorno. Come si chiama? — Mi chiamo Marco Rossi. E Lei? — Rossi. Molto piacere.
io — "I" ( from ego), usually dropped — the verb ending carries it.
mi chiamo — "I call myself" (chiamarsi from clāmāre, "call out"; kin of Spanish me llamo, Portuguese me chamo).
Come ti chiami? / Come si chiama? — "how do you call yourself?", informal / formal.
piacere — "a pleasure" ( from placēre; twin of Portuguese prazer).

segments.prompt: Why can Italian usually omit io?
acceptedResponses: the verb ending identifies the subject
the verb ending carries the subject

feedback.correct: Right: the verb ending already identifies the subject, so io is often unnecessary.
